summary: Describes how the RFC Series and the RFC Editor function are organized, with community involvement and accountability as the Internet technical community grew. It lays out the framework that lets the series keep fulfilling its purpose as the publisher of Internet technical documents. It is informational and was later replaced by RFC 8729.

plainLanguage.summary: The RFC Series is the archive of Internet technical documents. This document explains how that archive is run: what the series is for, who does what, and where the boundaries are between the RFC Editor, the IAB and the bodies that feed documents in. It also names the four streams of input and says who approves documents in each.

questions: how is the rfc series run
what is the independent submission stream
subtitle: The rules that keep the RFC Series a single series while several different communities feed it.

tldr.problem: Several different groups contribute documents to the RFC Series, each with its own approval rules, and it was not clear where community involvement should stop and RFC Editor control begin.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC divides the work into four activities, names the bodies responsible for each, and defines four streams, each with its own approving body, under one mission and one framework for changing the rules.
tldr.outcome: The series keeps a single archival identity while the streams stay separate. RFC 4844 was obsoleted by RFC 8729.

sections.title: Why the Series Needed a Framework
sections.content:
The first Request for Comments document was published in April of 1969 as part of the effort to design and build what is now known as the Internet. Since then the RFC Series has been the archival series dedicated to documenting Internet technical specifications, including general contributions from the Internet research and engineering community as well as standards documents. The series was created to capture the research and engineering thought that underlies the design of the Internet. As the IETF was formalized to carry out the discussion and documentation of Internet standards, IETF documents became a large part, but not the entirety, of the series.

As the IETF has grown, its requirements for archival publication of its output have changed and become more rigorous. Perhaps most significantly, the IETF must be able to define, based on its own open consensus discussion processes and leadership directions, and implement adjustments to its publication processes.

At the same time, the Internet engineering and research community as a whole has grown and come to require more openness and accountability in all organizations supporting it. The community needs an RFC Series that is supported, operationally and in terms of its principles, so that there is a balance of expert implementation, clear management and direction across the whole series whether originating in the IETF or not, and appropriate community input into and review of activities.

The RFC names the problem plainly: there is confusion and therefore sometimes tension over where and how to address RFC issues particular to contributing groups such as the IETF, the IAB or independent individuals. It is not clear where there should be community involvement rather than RFC Editor control, and depending on the issue there might be more or less involvement from the IAB, the IESG or the community at large. The same applies to series-wide issues, such as intellectual property rights for IETF-generated documents, where the portions relevant to the rest of the series have to be extracted somehow. Without an agreed framework, such discussions become polarised, with either the IETF dictating reality for the whole series or the series imposing undue restrictions on the IETF document series.
sections.plainLanguage: The series has grown from a single person's letterhead into an archive fed by several communities with different rules. The problem this document solves is who decides what: the communities that write documents, or the editor who publishes them. The answer given is a framework that separates the parts clearly.

sections.title: The RFC Series Mission
sections.content:
The RFC Series is the archival series dedicated to documenting Internet technical specifications, including general contributions from the Internet research and engineering community as well as standards documents.

RFCs are available free of charge to anyone via the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: The mission has two parts: archive the technical specifications that describe the Internet, and make them free for anyone to read. Everything else in the document is about how to keep that promise while the number of contributors and the volume of work keep growing.

sections.title: Roles and Responsibilities
sections.content:
Originally there was a single person acting as editor of the RFC Series. The task has grown, and the work now requires the organised activity of several experts, so there are RFC Editors, or an RFC Editor organisation, and in time there may be multiple organisations working together. For simplicity the document refers to this collection of experts and organisations as the RFC Editor, which is the implementer handling the editorial management of the series in accordance with the defined processes, and is expected to be the expert and prime mover in discussions about policies for editing, publishing and archiving RFCs.

The role of the IAB is to ensure that the RFC Series mission is being appropriately fulfilled for the whole community for which it was created. The IAB does not, organisationally, have comprehensive publishing or editorial expertise, so its role is focused on ensuring that principles are met, the appropriate bodies and communities are duly informed and consulted, and the RFC Editor has what it needs to execute on the material in its mandate. It is the responsibility of the IAB to approve the appointment of the RFC Editor and to approve the general policy followed by the RFC Editor.

The IETF Administrative Support Activity, created under BCP 101, provides administrative support for the IETF, the IAB and the IRTF. In its role of supporting the IAB it is tasked with providing the funding for and operational oversight of the RFC Editor. The IAOC, the IETF Administrative Oversight Committee, is the oversight board of the IASA, and the IAD, the IETF Administrative Director, is the chief actor for the IASA. The IAOC works with the IAB to identify suitable persons or entities to fulfil the mandate of the RFC Editor, establishes contractual agreements with them to carry out the work that satisfies the technical publication requirements defined for the various RFC input streams, and may define additional operational requirements and policies for management purposes. It also provides oversight of the operation of the RFC Editor activity based on the established agreements.

On policy oversight, the IAB monitors the effectiveness of the policies in force and their implementation, to ensure that the RFC Editor activity meets the editorial management and document publication needs set out in the document. In the event of serious non-conformance, the IAB, on its own initiative or at the request of the IAOC, may require the IAOC to vary or terminate and renegotiate the arrangements for the RFC Editor activity.
sections.plainLanguage: Four bodies share the work. The RFC Editor does the editing and publishing. The IAB sets the policy and appoints the editor. The IAOC, a committee inside the Internet Society's administrative arm, funds the editor and signs the contract. The IAD runs that administrative arm day to day.

sections.title: The Framework
sections.content:
The framework describes the operational implementation of the RFC Series, based on public process and definition documents, for which there are clear responsibilities and mechanisms for update and change. Generally speaking, the RFC Editor is responsible for the operational implementation, and the IAD provides the oversight of that operational role.

The process and definition documents are maintained with the appropriate community so that they reflect current requirements. The IAB is charged with verifying that appropriate community input has been sought and that any changes appropriately account for community requirements.

There are three categories of activity, and a fourth category of series-wide rules and guidelines: approval of documents; editing, processing and publication of documents; archiving and indexing the documents and making them accessible; and series rules and guidelines.

For document approval, each stream has its own documented approval process, and there is generally a different approving body for each stream. The RFC Editor is responsible for approval of documents in one stream, the Independent Submission stream, and works with the other approving bodies to ensure smooth passage of approved documents into the next phases.

For editing, processing and publication, producing and maintaining a coherent, well-edited series requires specialised skills and subject matter expertise, which is the domain of the RFC Editor. General and stream-specific requirements are documented in community-approved documents, and any specific interfaces, numbers or concrete values needed to make the requirements operational are the subject of agreements between the IASA and the RFC Editor, such as contracts, statements of work or service level agreements.

For archiving, indexing and accessibility, in principle there should be a community consensus document describing the requirements, but in practice the archive built by the capable RFC Editors since the series' inception continues to be used. There are no applicable process documents for this category. For series-wide rules and guidelines, there should be uniform style and content across all streams, covering acceptable language, use of references and copyright rules. The existing rules and guidelines documents are Instructions to RFC Authors (RFC 2223), copyright and intellectual property rules (RFC 3978 and RFC 4748), and normative references (RFC 3967 and RFC 4897).
sections.plainLanguage: The work is split into four buckets: deciding that a document is ready, editing and publishing it, keeping the archive and its index usable, and setting the rules that apply to every document in the series. Each bucket has a named owner, and each has a rule for how it may be changed, with the IAB checking that the community was consulted first.

sections.title: The RFC Streams
sections.content:
Various contributors provide input to the RFC Series, coming from several different communities, each with its own defined process for approving documents that will be published by the RFC Editor. Over time these communities and their document requirements have grown and separated, and it is useful to recognise each in its own space. The document calls these streams. By identifying separate streams there is no intention of dividing them or undermining their management as one series; the opposite is true, because clarifying the constituent parts makes it easier for them to work together without the friction that sometimes arises when discussing various requirements. There is no immediate expectation of new streams being created, and it is preferable that new streams not be created.

Processes for approval of documents in each stream are defined by the community that defines the stream, and the IAB verifies that appropriate community input has been sought and that changes are consistent with the RFC Series mission. The RFC Editor is expected to publish all documents passed to it after appropriate review and approval in one of the identified streams.

The IETF document stream includes IETF working group documents and individual submissions sponsored by an IESG area director. Any document published as part of the IETF standards process must follow this stream, and no other stream can approve Standards-Track or Best Current Practice RFCs. Its approval process is defined by the IETF standards process and the IESG process for sponsoring individual submissions. The IAB document stream uses the IAB process for review and approval of its documents, and any IAB documents the IAB wishes to publish as part of the Standards Track are subject to the IETF stream's approval processes. The IRTF document stream exists because the IRTF is chartered as an activity of the IAB, and with the approval of the IAB the IRTF may publish and update a process for publication of its own, non-Standards-Track documents. The Independent Submission stream exists because the RFC Series has always served a broader technical community than the IETF; it provides review and, where appropriate, approval of documents outside the scope of the other streams, and approval there falls under the purview of the RFC Editor, who seeks input from the IESG.

Each stream also has technical publication requirements, which the community behind each stream outlines. The IAB must agree that the requirements are consistent with and implementable as part of the RFC Editor activity. The requirements for the IETF stream are defined in RFC 4714, and the other three streams identify the applicable requirements in RFC 4714, deviating only minimally if they elect to define others.
sections.plainLanguage: Documents arrive through four doors: the IETF, the IAB, the IRTF, and the independent submission stream for work from outside the IETF. Each door has its own approver, and only the IETF door can approve standards-track or Best Current Practice documents. The point of naming them separately is to stop the friction, not to split the archive.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The processes for the publication of documents must prevent the introduction of unapproved changes. Since the RFC Editor maintains the index of publications, sufficient security must be in place to prevent these published documents from being changed by external parties. The archive of RFC documents, any source documents needed to recreate the RFC documents, and any associated original documents, such as lists of errata, tools and, for some early items, non-machine-readable originals, need to be secured against failure of the storage medium and other similar disasters.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things need protecting: the published documents, so that nobody can quietly edit a published RFC, and the stored originals, so that a broken disk does not destroy the archive. The RFC Editor keeps the index, which makes the first point the editor's responsibility.

items.text: The oversight board of the IASA. It funds the RFC Editor and contracts with whoever does the work.
